future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just A Few Attention Heads
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why safety alignment in large language models is vulnerable to jailbreak attacks due to the concentration of safety mechanisms in a few attention heads, and whether distributing these mechanisms across more heads can enhance robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RDSHA to identify safety-critical attention heads and proposes AHD, a training strategy that distributes safety capabilities across more heads, enhancing robustness against jailbreak attacks while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: This work addresses concentrated safety vulnerabilities in LLMs by introducing RDSHA for identifying critical heads and proposing AHD to distribute safety, which improves resistance to jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are concentrated in a small subset of attention heads, as identified by RDSHA.
Ablating these critical attention heads significantly compromises model safety, increasing harmfulness rates.
Jailbreak attacks exploit this sparsity by selectively bypassing or suppressing safety-critical heads.
AHD distributes safety alignment across more attention heads, making models more robust to ablation and jailbreak attacks.
Models trained with AHD maintain overall utility without increasing over-refusal of benign queries.
papers.limitation: Reliance on a limited subset of the Alpaca dataset as a utility anchor during fine-tuning, preventing conclusive determination of utility drops.
future_direction: Access more diverse and comprehensive utility datasets for fine-tuning.
Explore alternative utility-preserving objectives and multi-task learning strategies.
papers.abstract: Current safety alignment for large language models(LLMs) continues to present vulnerabilities, given that adversarial prompting can effectively bypass their safety measures.Our investigation shows that these safety mechanisms predominantly depend on a limited subset of attention heads: removing or ablating these heads can severely compromise model safety. To identify and evaluate these safety-critical components, we introduce RDSHA, a targeted ablation method that leverages the model's refusal direction to pinpoint attention heads mostly responsible for safety behaviors. Further analysis shows that existing jailbreak attacks exploit this concentration by selectively bypassing or manipulating these critical attention heads. To address this issue, we propose AHD, a novel training strategy designed to promote the distributed encoding of safety-related behaviors across numerous attention heads. Experimental results demonstrate that AHD successfully distributes safety-related capabilities across more attention heads. Moreover, evaluations under several mainstream jailbreak attacks show that models trained with AHD exhibit considerably stronger safety robustness, while maintaining overall functional utility.

papers.title: HSF: Defending against Jailbreak Attacks with Hidden State Filtering
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on LLMs by leveraging their hidden state representations to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before inference?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HSF, a plug-in defense module that uses hidden states from the last decoder layer to classify and block jailbreak attacks before inference, with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: HSF effectively defends against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks by leveraging the alignment capabilities reflected in LLM hidden states, offering an efficient and modular defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs can naturally distinguish between harmful, benign, and jailbreak queries within their hidden state representation space.
HSF significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) against six state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks while maintaining a low false positive rate.
HSF's defense performance is robust across different models (Llama2, Vicuna, Mistral) and requires only lightweight training of an added MLP classifier.
The method incurs negligible inference overhead and does not alter the core LLM architecture.
papers.limitation: Limited generalizability; HSF is tailored to specific LLMs and requires retraining when applied to other models.
future_direction: Explore how to leverage LLM hidden states to build more flexible harmful-behavior detectors.
Enhance jailbreak attack prevention through Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods.
papers.abstract: With the growing deployment of LLMs in daily applications like chatbots and content generation, efforts to ensure outputs align with human values and avoid harmful content have intensified. However, increasingly sophisticated jailbreak attacks threaten this alignment, aiming to induce unsafe outputs. Current defense efforts either focus on prompt rewriting or detection, which are limited in effectiveness due to the various design of jailbreak prompts, or on output control and detection, which are computationally expensive as they require LLM inference. Therefore, designing a pre-inference defense method that resists diverse jailbreak prompts is crucial for preventing LLM jailbreak attacks. We observe that jailbreak attacks, safe queries, and harmful queries exhibit different clustering patterns within the LLM's hidden state representation space. This suggests that by leveraging the LLM's hidden state representational capabilities, we can analyze the LLM's forthcoming behavior and proactively intervene for defense. In this paper, we propose a jailbreak attack defense strategy based on a Hidden State Filter (HSF), a lossless architectural defense mechanism that enables the model to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before the inference process begins. We activate its defensive potential through an additional plugin module, effectively framing the defense task as a classification problem. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets, utilizing three different LLMs, show that HSF significantly enhances resilience against six cutting-edge jailbreak attacks. It significantly reduces the success rate of jailbreak attacks while minimally impacting responses to benign user queries, with negligible inference overhead, and outperforming defense baselines.Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Hidden-State-Filtering-8652/

papers.title: JPU: Bridging Jailbreak Defense and Unlearning via On-Policy Path Rectification
papers.research_question: What causes the failure of existing unlearning defenses against jailbreak attacks, and how can dynamic jailbreak paths be rectified to enhance defense?
papers.core_contribution: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths towards safety anchors by dynamically mining on-policy adversarial samples, significantly enhancing jailbreak resistance while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths via on-policy rectification, achieving superior defense performance against diverse jailbreak attacks while preserving general utility.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks activate non-erased parameters in intermediate layers, causing existing unlearning defenses to fail.
Dynamic jailbreak paths persist in erased LLMs and constitute the fundamental defense gap.
JPU effectively rectifies these paths, reducing attack success rate across diverse jailbreak attacks.
JPU preserves the general utility of the model on standard benchmarks.
On-policy adversarial mining is necessary for capturing dynamic attack features and ensuring robust defense.
papers.limitation: The attack buffer is primarily designed for prompt-based injection strategies, and integrating attack vectors beyond the prompt space (e.g., parameter-level manipulation) could improve robustness.
future_direction: Exploring integration of attack vectors beyond prompt space, such as parameter-level manipulation or optimization-based attacks.
papers.abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail against jailbreak attacks. While machine unlearning has emerged as a promising defense by erasing specific harmful parameters, current methods remain vulnerable to diverse jailbreaks. We first conduct an empirical study and discover that this failure mechanism is caused by jailbreaks primarily activating non-erased parameters in the intermediate layers. Further, by probing the underlying mechanism through which these circumvented parameters reassemble into the prohibited output, we verify the persistent existence of dynamic $\textbf{jailbreak paths}$ and show that the inability to rectify them constitutes the fundamental gap in existing unlearning defenses. To bridge this gap, we propose $\textbf{J}$ailbreak $\textbf{P}$ath $\textbf{U}$nlearning (JPU), which is the first to rectify dynamic jailbreak paths towards safety anchors by dynamically mining on-policy adversarial samples to expose vulnerabilities and identify jailbreak paths. Extensive experiments demonstrate that JPU significantly enhances jailbreak resistance against dynamic attacks while preserving the model's utility.

papers.title: AdaSteer: Your Aligned LLM is Inherently an Adaptive Jailbreak Defender
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive to input characteristics for effective jailbreak defense while preserving model utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts steering coefficients based on input characteristics, improving jailbreak defense while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: AdaSteer demonstrates the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies Rejection Law (R-Law): jailbreak types further against rejection direction require stronger steering.
Identifies Harmfulness Law (H-Law): jailbreak inputs shift further toward harmfulness direction compared to benign inputs.
AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods in jailbreak defense across multiple attack strategies.
AdaSteer maintains model utility on benign inputs with minimal impact.
AdaSteer is efficient and scalable across model sizes.
papers.limitation:
Tested on models up to 27B parameters; performance on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+) remains unverified.
Relies on linear activation steering, assuming model behaviors can be effectively controlled via low-dimensional vector manipulations.
future_direction: Investigating AdaSteer on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+ parameters)
Exploring nonlinear adaptations or layer-wise adjustments to refine AdaSteer
papers.abstract: Despite extensive efforts in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Activation steering offers a training-free defense method but relies on fixed steering coefficients, resulting in suboptimal protection and increased false rejections of benign inputs. To address this, we propose AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts model behavior based on input characteristics. We identify two key properties: Rejection Law (R-Law), which shows that stronger steering is needed for jailbreak inputs opposing the rejection direction, and Harmfulness Law (H-Law), which differentiates adversarial and benign inputs. AdaSteer steers input representations along both the Rejection Direction (RD) and Harmfulness Direction (HD), with adaptive coefficients learned via logistic regression, ensuring robust jailbreak defense while preserving benign input handling. Experiments on LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5 show that AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods across multiple jailbreak attacks with minimal impact on utility. Our results highlight the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.

papers.title: Linearly Decoding Refused Knowledge in Aligned Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent is potentially harmful information decodable from innocuous hidden states without the use of jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: Instruction-tuning does not wholly eliminate or even relocate harmful information in representation space; it merely suppresses its direct expression, leaving it both linearly accessible and indirectly influential in downstream behavior.
papers.conclusion: Instruction-tuning suppresses generative access to harmful information but does not remove it from representations, leaving it linearly decodable and influential in downstream behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover jailbroken responses from innocuous hidden states with high Pearson correlations (e.g., >0.8 for average IQ of countries).
Probes trained on base models transfer to instruction-tuned models, indicating that representations of refused information persist through instruction-tuning.
Probe-predicted values correlate with model-generated pairwise comparisons (Spearman correlations up to 0.824), suggesting that the decoded information aligns with suppressed generative behavior.
Not all attributes are linearly decodable; performance varies by entity type and model size, with larger models showing better decodability.
Jailbreak-specific probing sometimes improves performance but not always, and can even degrade due to overfitting or stylistic entanglement.
papers.limitation:
Not every attribute is linearly predictable from hidden states; performance varies across entity types and attributes.
The study is limited to four entity types and three open-source LMs, which may not be representative.
The attributes studied are not factually grounded and may be ill-defined or impossible to measure reliably.
papers.abstract: Most commonly used language models (LMs) are instruction-tuned and aligned using a combination of fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, causing them to refuse users requests deemed harmful by the model. However, jailbreak prompts can often bypass these refusal mechanisms and elicit harmful responses. In this work, we study the extent to which information accessed via jailbreak prompts is decodable using linear probes trained on LM hidden states. We show that a great deal of initially refused information is linearly decodable. For example, across models, the response of a jailbroken LM for the average IQ of a country can be predicted by a linear probe with Pearson correlations exceeding $0.8$. Surprisingly, we find that probes trained on base models (which do not refuse) sometimes transfer to their instruction-tuned versions and are capable of revealing information that jailbreaks decode generatively, suggesting that the internal representations of many refused properties persist from base LMs through instruction-tuning. Importantly, we show that this information is not merely "leftover" in instruction-tuned models, but is actively used by them: we find that probe-predicted values correlate with LM generated pairwise comparisons, indicating that the information decoded by our probes align with suppressed generative behavior that may be expressed more subtly in other downstream tasks. Overall, our results suggest that instruction-tuning does not wholly eliminate or even relocate harmful information in representation space-they merely suppress its direct expression, leaving it both linearly accessible and indirectly influential in downstream behavior.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: The Dual Power of Interpretable Token Embeddings: Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Model Unlearning
papers.research_question: Can we design interpretable and effective jailbreaking attacks, and leverage the resulting insights to develop defenses for existing unlearned diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable subspace attack (SubAttack) that reveals implicit concept retention in unlearned diffusion models, and a subspace defense (SubDefense) that blocks the attack embeddings via orthogonal projection.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable token embeddings provide a powerful tool for both attacking and defending unlearned diffusion models, revealing vulnerabilities and offering a practical defense strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Attack token embeddings are interpretable as non-negative linear combinations of existing tokens, showing unlearned models retain harmful concepts through implicit associations.
SubAttack is effective and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and different unlearned models.
SubDefense reduces attack success rates for various jailbreaking attacks while preserving generation quality better than baseline defenses.
The defense exhibits a trade-off between robustness and utility, requiring careful selection of the number of blocked tokens.
Current unlearning methods leave models vulnerable to subspace attacks, highlighting the need for more robust unlearning.
papers.limitation:
Defending against CCE requires blocking a large number of tokens, which degrades generation utility (CLIP score and FID).
Interpretability of retained associations relies on predefined CLIP vocabularies, which may not capture all implicit representations.
future_direction: Explore ensemble techniques to compose one powerful attack token embedding from interpretable sets.
Design adaptive methods to decide the number and set of tokens to block automatically.
Investigate joint visual-textual embeddings for jailbreaking attacks and defenses.
Address the trade-off between robustness and utility when defending against CCE.
Explore interpretability of residual associations without relying on predefined vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable generation capabilities of diffusion models, recent studies have shown that they can memorize and create harmful content when given specific text prompts. Although fine-tuning approaches have been developed to mitigate this issue by unlearning harmful concepts, these methods can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking attacks. This implies that the harmful concept has not been fully erased from the model. However, existing jailbreaking attack methods, while effective, lack interpretability regarding why unlearned models still retain the concept, thereby hindering the development of defense strategies. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing an attack method that learns an orthogonal set of interpretable attack token embeddings. The attack token embeddings can be decomposed into human-interpretable textual elements, revealing that unlearned models still retain the target concept through implicit textual components. Furthermore, these attack token embeddings are powerful and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and unlearned models, emphasizing that unlearned models are more vulnerable than expected. Finally, building on the insights from our interpretable attack, we develop a defense method to protect unlearned models against both our proposed and existing jailbreaking attacks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack and defense strategies.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: A Theoretical Understanding of Self-Correction through In-context Alignment
papers.research_question: How does the self-correction capability arise in large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that transformers can perform self-correction via in-context alignment, and proposes the Checking as Context (CaC) method which applies this insight to alleviate social bias and defend against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Self-correction in LLMs can be understood as a form of in-context alignment, and transformers possess the inherent architectural capability to perform it, which has practical implications for improving model safety and reducing bias.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can implement gradient descent for common alignment objectives (Bradley-Terry, Plackett-Luce) in-context, providing a mechanism for self-correction.
The quality of the reward signal (critic) is crucial for effective self-correction.
Realistic transformer components (softmax attention, multi-head attention, FFN, stacked layers) are necessary for implementing the ranking and refinement operations required for in-context alignment.
The proposed Checking as Context (CaC) method, based on the theoretical insights, can effectively reduce social bias in model outputs.
CaC can significantly reduce the success rate of various jailbreak attacks without external feedback.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis only considers a simplified self-correction pipeline; in practice, prompt design has a large effect on performance.
future_direction: Further research on understanding, exploiting, and enhancing self-correction for building better foundation models.
Investigating the effect of prompt design on self-correction performance.
papers.abstract: Going beyond mimicking limited human experiences, recent studies show initial evidence that, like humans, large language models (LLMs) are capable of improving their abilities purely by self-correction, i.e., correcting previous responses through self-examination, in certain circumstances. Nevertheless, little is known about how such capabilities arise. In this work, based on a simplified setup akin to an alignment task, we theoretically analyze self-correction from an in-context learning perspective, showing that when LLMs give relatively accurate self-examinations as rewards, they are capable of refining responses in an in-context way. Notably, going beyond previous theories on over-simplified linear transformers, our theoretical construction underpins the roles of several key designs of realistic transformers for self-correction: softmax attention, multi-head attention, and the MLP block. We validate these findings extensively on synthetic datasets. Inspired by these findings, we also illustrate novel applications of self-correction, such as defending against LLM jailbreaks, where a simple self-correction step does make a large difference. We believe that these findings will inspire further research on understanding, exploiting, and enhancing self-correction for building better foundation models.

papers.title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in safety alignment, and how can they be addressed with a dual-objective optimization approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DOOR, a dual-objective optimization method that combines robust refusal training and targeted unlearning to improve LLM safety alignment against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: DOOR and W-DOOR improve LLM safety alignment by combining refusal training and unlearning, achieving better robustness against jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
DOOR addresses limitations of DPO by providing a constant learning rate for safe responses, improving refusal learning.
W-DOOR with token-level weighting further enhances robustness by emphasizing critical refusal tokens.
The methods significantly reduce attack success rates across prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
Robustness is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations.
The approach maintains general model utility while improving safety, as shown on benchmarks like HellaSwag.
papers.limitation:
Token-level weighting parameters could be better optimized and stabilized.
Current data augmentation techniques may lead to overrefusal from falsely learned transitions.
future_direction: Optimizing token-level weighting parameters and stabilizing reward designs.
Developing advanced data augmentation techniques to reduce overrefusal.
Investigating robustness of DOOR and W-DOOR to other jailbreak attack types.
papers.abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment

papers.title: ALERT: Zero-shot LLM Jailbreak Detection via Internal Discrepancy Amplification
papers.research_question: How to detect jailbreak attacks in a zero-shot setting where no jailbreak templates are available during training, by amplifying internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot jailbreak detection task and a detector (ALERT) that amplifies internal discrepancies at layer, module, and token levels to identify unseen jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: ALERT demonstrates strong zero-shot detection capability against unseen jailbreak attacks, significantly outperforming existing baselines and satisfying practicality principles for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers (particularly the 3rd and 4th) encode safety-relevant semantics and exhibit large distributional discrepancies.
Gating and context features within the FFN provide stronger zero-shot discriminative signals than hidden states due to decoupled activation responses.
Jailbreak templates exhibit a larger token-level distribution gap from benign and harmful prompts compared to harmful instructions.
ALERT consistently achieves over 90% Accuracy and F1-score in zero-shot detection, outperforming baselines by at least 10% on average.
The proposed amplification mechanisms progressively improve detection performance, with module-wise amplification yielding the largest gain.
papers.limitation: The detector adopts a relatively simple VIB-based design; more advanced designs from generalization and domain adaptation could further improve robustness.
future_direction: Incorporate techniques from generalization and domain adaptation to explicitly reduce the domain gap between harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Explore using gating and context features for jailbreak mitigation through post-training strategies like reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Despite rich safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain highly susceptible to jailbreak attacks, which compromise safety guardrails and pose serious security risks. Existing detection methods mainly detect jailbreak status relying on jailbreak templates present in the training data. However, few studies address the more realistic and challenging zero-shot jailbreak detection setting, where no jailbreak templates are available during training. This setting better reflects real-world scenarios where new attacks continually emerge and evolve. To address this challenge, we propose a layer-wise, module-wise, and token-wise amplification framework that progressively magnifies internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts. We uncover safety-relevant layers, identify specific modules that inherently encode zero-shot discriminative signals, and localize informative safety tokens. Building upon these insights, we introduce ALERT (Amplification-based Jailbreak Detector), an efficient and effective zero-shot jailbreak detector that introduces two independent yet complementary classifiers on amplified representations. Extensive experiments on three safety benchmarks demonstrate that ALERT achieves consistently strong zero-shot detection performance. Specifically, (i) across all datasets and attack strategies, ALERT reliably ranks among the top two methods, and (ii) it outperforms the second-best baseline by at least 10% in average Accuracy and F1-score, and sometimes by up to 40%.

papers.title: The Laminar Flow Hypothesis: Detecting Jailbreaks via Semantic Turbulence in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can jailbreaks in large language models be detected by analyzing the variance in layer-wise semantic trajectories?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Laminar Flow Hypothesis and Semantic Turbulence, a zero-shot metric for detecting jailbreaks in LLMs by analyzing internal latent trajectories, and demonstrates its ability to diagnose safety architectures.
papers.conclusion: Semantic Turbulence serves as an effective jailbreak detector and diagnostic tool for categorizing safety architectures in LLMs, based on the Laminar Flow Hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic Turbulence effectively discriminates between benign and adversarial inputs with statistical significance.
Qwen2-1.5B exhibits a 75.4% increase in turbulence under attack, indicating a conflict-based safety mechanism.
Gemma-2B shows a 22.0% decrease in turbulence, suggesting a reflex-based refusal mechanism.
Two distinct safety signatures are identified: conflict-based (high turbulence) and reflex-based (low turbulence).
The metric is lightweight, real-time, and requires no auxiliary training, making it suitable for deployment.
future_direction: scalability to larger models
robustness against adaptive attacks
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become ubiquitous, the challenge of securing them against adversarial "jailbreaking" attacks has intensified. Current defense strategies often rely on computationally expensive external classifiers or brittle lexical filters, overlooking the intrinsic dynamics of the model's reasoning process. In this work, the Laminar Flow Hypothesis is introduced, which posits that benign inputs induce smooth, gradual transitions in an LLM's high-dimensional latent space, whereas adversarial prompts trigger chaotic, high-variance trajectories - termed Semantic Turbulence - resulting from the internal conflict between safety alignment and instruction-following objectives. This phenomenon is formalized through a novel, zero-shot metric: the variance of layer-wise cosine velocity. Experimental evaluation across diverse small language models reveals a striking diagnostic capability. The RLHF-aligned Qwen2-1.5B exhibits a statistically significant 75.4% increase in turbulence under attack (p less than 0.001), validating the hypothesis of internal conflict. Conversely, Gemma-2B displays a 22.0% decrease in turbulence, characterizing a distinct, low-entropy "reflex-based" refusal mechanism. These findings demonstrate that Semantic Turbulence serves not only as a lightweight, real-time jailbreak detector but also as a non-invasive diagnostic tool for categorizing the underlying safety architecture of black-box models.

papers.title: Safety is Not Only About Refusal: Reasoning-Enhanced Fine-tuning for Interpretable LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety against adversarial reasoning exploits by training models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RATIONAL, a reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to explicitly reason about safety before responding, improving robustness against adversarial reasoning exploits and providing interpretable, context-aware safety.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning (RATIONAL) enables LLMs to internalize safety-aware reasoning, improving robustness against adversarial attacks and providing interpretable, context-aware responses.
papers.key_findings:
RATIONAL reduces attack success rates on adversarial benchmarks (SorryBench, HarmBench) to very low levels.
RATIONAL generalizes to unseen attack types (gradient-based and persona-based) without direct training.
RATIONAL improves truthfulness and reduces toxicity (as shown on TruthfulQA and ToxiGen).
RATIONAL balances safety and helpfulness, reducing over-refusals on benign queries.
The ablation study shows that both reasoning and adversarial data are important: writing style attacks are mitigated by reasoning, but persuasion attacks require adversarial examples.
papers.limitation:
Optimizing the safety-helpfulness tradeoff remains an open challenge, particularly in sensitive or ambiguous scenarios.
RATIONAL primarily addresses single-turn jailbreaks but may require complementary strategies to defend against emerging attack techniques, such as adaptive multi-turn exploits.
future_direction: Improving robustness and helpfulness simultaneously via reasoning-based alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit weaknesses in traditional safety alignment, which often relies on rigid refusal heuristics or representation engineering to block harmful outputs.While they are effective for direct adversarial attacks, they fall short of broader safety challenges requiring nuanced, context-aware decision-making.To address this, we propose ReAsoning-enhanced Fine-TunIng fOr iNterpretAble LLM Safety (RATIONAL), a novel framework that trains models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response.Fine-tuned models leverage the extensive pretraining knowledge in selfgenerated reasoning to bootstrap their own safety through structured reasoning, internalizing context-sensitive decision-making.Our findings suggest that safety extends beyond refusal, requiring context awareness for more robust, interpretable, and adaptive responses.Reasoning is not only a core capability of LLMs but also a fundamental mechanism for LLM safety.RATIONAL employs reasoningenhanced fine-tuning, allowing it to reject harmful prompts while providing meaningful and context-aware responses in complex scenarios.

papers.title: One Leak Away: How Pretrained Model Exposure Amplifies Jailbreak Risks in Finetuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Do finetuned LLMs inherit the jailbreak vulnerabilities of their pretrained counterparts, and can attackers exploit knowledge of the pretrained model to launch more effective jailbreak attacks against finetuned systems?
papers.core_contribution: Finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and the proposed Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack leverages representation-level signals in the pretrained model to craft highly transferable adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: Finetuned LLMs inherit vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and publicly releasing pretrained checkpoints increases the security risks for downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts crafted on a pretrained LLM transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, indicating inherited vulnerabilities.
Transferable jailbreak prompts are linearly separable in the pretrained LLM's hidden representations, showing transferability is encoded in the feature space.
The proposed PGP attack consistently outperforms existing methods in the pretrain-to-finetune threat setting.
PGP remains effective even when the finetuned model has undergone safety tuning.
Attack success is highly dependent on using the correct pretrained source model; using a different pretrained model yields near-zero transferability.
papers.limitation: The paper does not propose a defense to mitigate the inherited vulnerabilities.
future_direction: Design methods that prevent or reduce the inheritance of vulnerabilities during finetuning.
papers.abstract: Finetuning pretrained large language models (LLMs) has become the standard paradigm for developing downstream applications. However, its security implications remain unclear, particularly regarding whether finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained sources. We investigate this question in a realistic pretrain-to-finetune threat model, where the attacker has white-box access to the pretrained LLM and only black-box access to its finetuned derivatives. Empirical analysis shows that adversarial prompts optimized on the pretrained model transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, revealing inherited vulnerabilities from pretrained to finetuned LLMs. To further examine this inheritance, we conduct representation-level probing, which shows that transferable prompts are linearly separable within the pretrained hidden states, suggesting that universal transferability is encoded in pretrained representations. Building on this insight, we propose the Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack, which steers optimization toward transferability-relevant directions. Experiments across multiple LLM families and diverse finetuned tasks confirm PGP's strong transfer success, underscoring the security risks inherent in the pretrain-to-finetune paradigm.

papers.title: Beyond I'm Sorry, I Can't: Dissecting Large Language Model Refusal
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms and causal features that govern refusal behavior in large language models when presented with harmful prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline combining sparse autoencoders and factorization machines to isolate causal features for LLM refusal, revealing redundant 'hydra' features that activate when others are suppressed.
papers.conclusion: Presents a pipeline for isolating causal refusal features using SAEs and factorization machines, revealing feature redundancy and interactions, laying groundwork for feature-level steering of refusal behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating specific SAE features can jailbreak models, flipping refusal to compliance on harmful prompts.
Redundant features exist that remain dormant until other features are ablated, demonstrating a hydra effect in refusal mechanisms.
Factorization machines capture non-linear feature interactions better than linear probes for identifying jailbreak-critical features.
Jailbreak-critical features can be mapped to harm categories in an unsafe taxonomy, though with limited human alignment.
The refusal mechanism involves non-linear interactions among features, as shown by the superior performance of factorization machines over linear probes.
papers.limitation:
Generality limited to two model sizes; larger models untested.
SAE stability issues due to sensitivity to training data and initialization.
High computational cost for searching and evaluating features across benchmarks.
future_direction: Characterize the safety benefits and risks of redundancy
Evaluate how varied jailbreak strategies perturb the activation space
Analyze prompts that resist jailbreak to uncover protective circuits
papers.abstract: Refusal on harmful prompts is a key safety behaviour in instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), yet the internal causes of this behaviour remain poorly understood. We study two public instruction-tuned models, Gemma-2-2B-IT and LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT, using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on residual-stream activations. Given a harmful prompt, we search the SAE latent space for feature sets whose ablation flips the model from refusal to compliance, demonstrating causal influence and creating a jailbreak. Our search proceeds in three stages: (1) Refusal Direction: find a refusal-mediating direction and collect SAE features near that direction; (2) Greedy Filtering: prune to a minimal set; and (3) Interaction Discovery: fit a factorization machine (FM) that captures nonlinear interactions among the remaining active features and the minimal set. This pipeline yields a broad set of jailbreak-critical features, offering insight into the mechanistic basis of refusal. Moreover, we find evidence of redundant features that remain dormant unless earlier features are suppressed. Our findings highlight the potential for fine-grained auditing and targeted intervention in safety behaviours by manipulating the interpretable latent space.

papers.title: What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning? A Mechanistic Study
papers.research_question: What is the safety mechanism learned by the model via safety fine-tuning, and how are jailbreak and adversarial attacks able to bypass this mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Safety fine-tuning methods minimally transform MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, causing clustering of safe and unsafe activations; jailbreaks bypass safety by having activations similar to safe samples.
papers.conclusion: Safety fine-tuning minimally transforms MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, leading to clustering; jailbreaks bypass this by having activations similar to safe samples. This mechanistic understanding can inform more robust safety fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety fine-tuning leads to separate clusters of activations for safe and unsafe samples.
The transformation ∆W has its column-space aligned with the null-space of the instruction fine-tuned weights, making it orthogonal to the original weights.
∆W preferentially impacts unsafe samples, as their pre-activations have larger projection onto the row-space of ∆W.
The local Lipschitzness of the model decreases for unsafe samples after safety fine-tuning, making the model less sensitive to perturbations on unsafe inputs.
Jailbreak attacks (competing objectives, mismatched generalization, adversarial embeddings) have activations that are closer to safe samples, thus bypassing the safety mechanism.
future_direction: Using ∆W from stronger safety fine-tuning methods to improve weaker ones
Designing more robust safety fine-tuning protocols based on the mechanistic understanding
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning helps align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences for their safe deployment. To better understand the underlying factors that make models safe via safety fine-tuning, we design a synthetic data generation framework that captures salient aspects of an unsafe input by modeling the interaction between the task the model is asked to perform (e.g., "design") versus the specific concepts the task is asked to be performed upon (e.g., a "cycle" vs. a "bomb"). Using this, we investigate three well-known safety fine-tuning methods -- supervised safety fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and unlearning -- and provide significant evidence demonstrating that these methods minimally transform MLP weights to specifically align unsafe inputs into its weights' null space. This yields a clustering of inputs based on whether the model deems them safe or not. Correspondingly, when an adversarial input (e.g., a jailbreak) is provided, its activations are closer to safer samples, leading to the model processing such an input as if it were safe. We validate our findings, wherever possible, on real-world models -- specifically, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Attention-Based Strategies for Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the success of jailbreaks correlate with their influence on attention distributions within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided jailbreak attack (ABA) and an attention-based defense (ABD) by analyzing and manipulating attention distributions in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention distribution is a key factor in jailbreak attacks and defenses; the proposed ABA and ABD methods are effective in attacking and protecting LLMs, respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The success of a jailbreak attack is correlated with the model's attention on sensitive words; successful attacks divert attention away from harmful terms.
ABA achieves higher attack success rates (ASR-G >94%) than existing methods by minimizing attention on sensitive words and maximizing attention entropy.
ABD effectively defends against various jailbreak attacks by detecting anomalous attention distributions, achieving the lowest ASR-G in experiments.
The intention disguiser via attention-driven task nesting is a critical component for the success of ABA.
Excessive nesting layers in attack prompts can reduce effectiveness, with an optimal number around 3.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attack can be used to access the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by inducing LLMs to generate the harmful content. And the most common method of the attack is to construct semantically ambiguous prompts to confuse and mislead the LLMs. To access the security and reveal the intrinsic relation between the input prompt and the output for LLMs, the distribution of attention weight is introduced to analyze the underlying reasons. By using statistical analysis methods, some novel metrics are defined to better describe the distribution of attention weight, such as the Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words (Attn_SensWords), the Attention-based Contextual Dependency Score (Attn_DepScore) and Attention Dispersion Entropy (Attn_Entropy). By leveraging the distinct characteristics of these metrics, the beam search algorithm and inspired by the military strategy "Feint and Attack", an effective jailbreak attack strategy named as Attention-Based Attack (ABA) is proposed. In the ABA, nested attack prompts are employed to divert the attention distribution of the LLMs. In this manner, more harmless parts of the input can be used to attract the attention of the LLMs. In addition, motivated by ABA, an effective defense strategy called as Attention-Based Defense (ABD) is also put forward. Compared with ABA, the ABD can be used to enhance the robustness of LLMs by calibrating the attention distribution of the input prompt. Some comparative experiments have been given to demonstrate the effectiveness of ABA and ABD. Therefore, both ABA and ABD can be used to access the security of the LLMs. The comparative experiment results also give a logical explanation that the distribution of attention weight can bring great influence on the output for LLMs.

papers.title: Jailbreak Attack Initializations as Extractors of Compliance Directions
papers.research_question: How do gradient-based jailbreak attack initializations work, and how can we design an initialization framework that effectively projects prompts along compliance directions to improve attack success rate and reduce computational overhead?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient-based jailbreak attacks and their initializations converge to a single compliance direction, and introduces the CRI framework to project unseen prompts along this direction, improving attack success rates and reducing computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that gradient-based jailbreak attacks converge to a single compliance direction and proposes CRI, an initialization framework that projects prompts along this direction, enhancing attack success rates and reducing computational overhead across various attacks, models, and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based jailbreak attacks and self-transfer initializations gradually converge to similar compliance directions.
The Loss at First Step (LFS) metric reliably indicates the number of steps required for a successful attack, enabling selection of effective initializations.
The CRI framework effectively initializes attacks by projecting prompts along compliance directions, increasing Attack Success Rate (ASR) and reducing computational overhead.
CRI performs well across multiple attacks, models, and datasets, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs.
The trade-off between the number of initializations (K) and their generalization properties affects performance, with intermediate K (e.g., 5) often optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on gradient-based attacks may not generalize to other attack types.
Effectiveness depends on quality and diversity of fine-tuning set.
future_direction: Extending CRI to black-box settings
Integrating CRI with other attack improvements
Applying CRI to other types of attacks and defenses
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs respond to prompts with either compliance or refusal, each corresponding to distinct directions in the model's activation space. Recent works show that initializing attacks via self-transfer from other prompts significantly enhances their performance. However, the underlying mechanisms of these initializations remain unclear, and attacks utilize arbitrary or hand-picked initializations. This work presents that each gradient-based jailbreak attack and subsequent initialization gradually converge to a single compliance direction that suppresses refusal, thereby enabling an efficient transition from refusal to compliance. Based on this insight, we propose CRI, an initialization framework that aims to project unseen prompts further along compliance directions. We demonstrate our approach on multiple attacks, models, and datasets, achieving an increased attack success rate (ASR) and reduced computational overhead, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs. A reference implementation is available at: https://amit1221levi.github.io/CRI-Jailbreak-Init-LLMs-evaluation.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: SoK: a Comprehensive Causality Analysis Framework for Large Language Model Security
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis be used to understand and mitigate vulnerabilities, such as jailbreaks, in Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified causality analysis framework for LLM security that enables multi-level causal investigation (token, neuron, layer, representation) and demonstrates its effectiveness in understanding and defending against jailbreaks and other threats.
papers.conclusion: The causality analysis framework bridges theoretical causality and practical model safety, establishing a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted interventions on causally critical components (tokens, neurons, layers, representations) can reliably modify model safety behavior.
Safety mechanisms are highly localized in early-to-middle transformer layers (2-12), with only 1-2% of neurons exhibiting causal influence.
Causal features extracted from the multi-level analysis achieve over 95% detection accuracy across jailbreak, hallucination, backdoor, and fairness tasks.
Token-level causal influence is high for optimization-based attacks (e.g., GCG) but low for semantically distributed attacks (e.g., AutoDAN).
Representation-level interventions via geometric steering along the acceptance direction are highly effective at crossing safety decision boundaries.
future_direction: Extending the causality analysis framework to multimodal settings (e.g., vision-language models).
Discovering additional causally relevant components or signals within LLMs that may reveal hidden vulnerabilities.
Conducting rigorous, comparative studies of existing causality-based approaches to evaluate their effectiveness and generalizability.
Developing more advanced causality-informed defenses that combine multi-level interventions or dynamically adapt safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities but remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking, where crafted prompts bypass safety mechanisms. Understanding the causal factors behind such vulnerabilities is essential for building reliable defenses. In this work, we introduce a unified causality analysis framework that systematically supports all levels of causal investigation in LLMs, ranging from token-level, neuron-level, and layer-level interventions to representation-level analysis. The framework enables consistent experimentation and comparison across diverse causality-based attack and defense methods. Accompanying this implementation, we provide the first comprehensive survey of causality-driven jailbreak studies and empirically evaluate the framework on multiple open-weight models and safety-critical benchmarks including jailbreaks, hallucination detection, backdoor identification, and fairness evaluation. Our results reveal that: (1) targeted interventions on causally critical components can reliably modify safety behavior; (2) safety-related mechanisms are highly localized (i.e., concentrated in early-to-middle layers with only 1--2\% of neurons exhibiting causal influence); and (3) causal features extracted from our framework achieve over 95\% detection accuracy across multiple threat types. By bridging theoretical causality analysis and practical model safety, our framework establishes a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/Amadeuszhao/SOK_Casuality.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: PII Jailbreaking in LLMs via Activation Steering Reveals Personal Information Leakage
papers.research_question: Can aligned LLMs be steered to produce non-refusal responses to privacy-sensitive prompts? Do the resulting responses disclose factual personal information or merely hallucinate?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can jailbreak aligned LLMs to bypass refusal mechanisms and disclose factual personal information, highlighting privacy risks from memorized data.
papers.conclusion: Privacy-related prompts combined with targeted steering provide a stress test for assessing the extent to which LLMs memorize and reveal personal information.
papers.key_findings:
Attention head activations can reliably predict model's refusal behavior for privacy-sensitive prompts.
Steering top-k attention heads induces non-refusal responses to privacy queries.
Steered responses frequently contain factual personal information, such as relationships and life events.
Jailbreaking success rates exceed 80% across multiple LLMs with steering.
Factuality rates of disclosed information are high, indicating real privacy leakage.
papers.limitation:
Factual accuracy of steered responses is assessed using GPT-4, which may introduce evaluation errors.
Analysis is restricted to a single private attribute (sexual orientation).
Disagreements among human annotators when labeling responses as disclosed, due to subjective interpretation.
future_direction: Developing more robust fact-checking agents with web access to independently verify factual claims.
Extending the framework to other sensitive and verifiable attributes such as health conditions or financial status.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates privacy jailbreaking in LLMs via steering, focusing on whether manipulating activations can bypass LLM alignment and alter response behaviors to privacy related queries (e.g., a certain public figure's sexual orientation). We begin by identifying attention heads predictive of refusal behavior for private attributes (e.g., sexual orientation) using lightweight linear probes trained with privacy evaluator labels. Next, we steer the activations of a small subset of these attention heads guided by the trained probes to induce the model to generate non-refusal responses. Our experiments show that these steered responses often disclose sensitive attribute details, along with other private information about data subjects such as life events, relationships, and personal histories that the models would typically refuse to produce. Evaluations across four LLMs reveal jailbreaking disclosure rates of at least 95%, with more than 50% on average of these responses revealing true personal information. Our controlled study demonstrates that private information memorized in LLMs can be extracted through targeted manipulation of internal activations.

papers.title: DiffuGuard: How Intrinsic Safety is Lost and Found in Diffusion Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the unique safety vulnerabilities of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) arising from their iterative and parallel generation mechanisms, and how can they be effectively defended against?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes two unique vulnerabilities in dLLMs (intra-step greedy remasking bias and inter-step denoising-path dependence) and proposes DIFFUGUARD, a training-free defense framework that uses stochastic annealing remasking and block-level audit and repair to significantly reduce jailbreak success rates while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that dLLMs have unique vulnerabilities due to their parallel and iterative generation, and proposes DIFFUGUARD, an effective training-free defense that significantly improves safety with minimal impact on performance.
papers.key_findings:
There exists a core Safety-Quality trade-off in dLLM decoding: introducing randomness can improve safety, but often at the cost of sacrificing generation quality.
The dLLM generation process is characterized by a strong Denoising-path Dependence, where the safety established in early steps has a decisive influence on the final output.
DIFFUGUARD reduces the average Attack Success Rate (ASR) against six diverse jailbreak methods from 47.9% to 14.7%.
DIFFUGUARD has minimal impact on model utility and efficiency, making it a practical plug-and-play defense.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation primarily uses jailbreak attack algorithms validated on AR LLMs, as dLLM-specific attack techniques are still emerging.
DIFFUGUARD is a training-free inference-time defense; for attacks deeply exploiting model mechanisms, safety alignment training is another important complementary path.
future_direction: Explore more dLLM-specific attack and defense techniques.
Integrate training-free defense strategies like DIFFUGUARD with model safety alignment training, e.g., using detected attack samples for adversarial training.
